rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.7 and 3; a two-season (2009, 2010) randomized block field experiment in a commercial drip-irrigated 'Manzanilla fina' olive orchard in La Rioja, Argentina, with four post-harvest irrigation levels (100, 66, 33, 0% ETc) and measurements of soil water, stem water potential, leaf conductance, sap flow and trunk diameter variations.
rows.notes: The study uses drip irrigation as the delivery system for all treatments but never measures soil evaporation, deep percolation or application efficiency, nor compares drip with any other application method. Its results concern responses of soil relative extractable water and plant water-stress indicators to deficit irrigation levels and the relationships among those indicators. It therefore provides no evidence of its own that drip controls soil evaporation or deep percolation; the only soil evaporation mention is a citation of earlier work (Rousseaux et al., 2009; Figuerola et al., 2013) in the introduction.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.7 and 3.5; own two-season field experiment with continuously recorded trunk dendrometers, periodic soil cores, pressure-chamber and porometer readings, and signal intensity / coefficient of variation / sensitivity analysis of each indicator.
rows.notes: The study evaluates the responsiveness and signal-to-noise of soil and plant indicators (including continuous dendrometer data) and concludes they show potential for scheduling irrigation, suggesting an REW threshold of about 48-50%. Irrigation was scheduled by the FAO56 method with fixed ETc fractions, not by sensors, automation or controllers, and no dynamic schedule adjustment or resulting water saving was implemented or measured. The study supports only a precondition (indicators could be used for scheduling), not the claimed delivery of dynamic schedule adjustment or water conservation by sensor/automation-based systems.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a primary field experiment on soil and plant water-stress indicators under post-harvest regulated deficit irrigation in a drip-irrigated olive orchard; neither claim row concerns an effect the study measured directly.
